name: Colin Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We’re independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a regular working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and supervise five people who compare supplier bids for a large home goods company. I check prices, delivery promises and contract changes before sending a recommendation upstairs. I only became a manager last year, and my best buyer still spots terms I miss. I like seeing a real shipment arrive at the price we agreed; I hate explaining a late order caused by a clause I skimmed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life at home like, and how much room would you have if the pay changed?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife, Mei, teaches at a preschool, and our children are six and thirteen. We have a mortgage, about three months of expenses saved, and my manager pay is normal for the job. There are some similar offices within a drive, though not a new vacancy every week. I have a bachelor’s degree and use AI now and then to compare bid tables after another buyer has checked the tool; I still trust a signed contract more than a summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the buyers to keep checking the signed terms and use a helper only where it saves time. A cheaper bid is no bargain if the delivery date is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be glad my job is still here, and three months saved gives our mortgage some cover. I still worry when Mei’s preschool has fewer paid days over a break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep the Monday bid review with my experienced buyer and use AI only to line up price tables before we read the contracts. In the first year Mei and I would set aside 110 monthly when her preschool pay is full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work and a little watchful about our bills. The ordinary school breaks still happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which contract term caught you out recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supplier could delay a sofa shipment without a price reduction. My buyer found the clause before we signed, and I thanked her in the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a newer tool in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after another buyer shows it against real bids. I’m willing to use something proven, but the signed page settles a dispute.

say: I’d keep **signed terms** at the centre of bid checks.
A low price cannot excuse a **wrong delivery date**.
think: Three months saved help with the **mortgage**, though school breaks still affect pay.
do: Keep **Monday bid reviews** and check AI price tables against contracts.
Save **110 monthly** only when Mei’s preschool pay is full.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and watchful about bills.
S0.quote: A cheaper bid is no bargain if the delivery date is wrong.
fieldNote: He uses AI **occasionally**, after another buyer checks it.
The household has a **three-month reserve** and a mortgage.
Mei’s **school-break pay** sets the condition for extra savings.

steps.text: Keep Monday bid reviews and compare AI price tables with signed contracts
Transfer 110 monthly to savings only when Mei’s preschool pay is full

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say writing and checking bids are exactly what the software will take first. We should compare its recommendations with deliveries before we let it approve a purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A smaller buying desk might not need a new manager who is still learning the clauses. I have savings and some other firms nearby, but those firms may also shrink buying teams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d test the tool on forty completed orders, noting every late shipment it would have missed. In the first year I’d take the paid supplier-audit course if my director funds the hours, and I’d ask for a posted on-site goods-checking role only if the pay covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the job, but the test feels manageable. I can learn what the tool gets wrong before betting the team on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help judge the forty orders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experienced buyer would check the delivery slips with me. She knows which supplier promises turn into boxes at the loading bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why on-site goods checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone still has to see whether the shipment matches the order. I know robots may enter hands-on work later, so I would treat that role as a bridge.

say: I’d test **bid recommendations** against delivered goods before software approves purchases.
The team needs **late-shipment counts** alongside any rollout plan.
think: A smaller desk could remove **my junior manager post**.
Nearby firms may have **similar cuts**, despite our reserve.
do: Test **forty completed orders** for missed delays.
Complete a **paid supplier-audit course** and seek posted goods-checking work at mortgage-covering pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to run a test.
S1.quote: Someone still has to see whether the shipment matches the order.
fieldNote: He checks **actual delivery slips**, not just software estimates.
His junior standing makes a **manager cut** plausible.
The course requires **paid hours**; a site role requires a viable posted wage.

steps.text: Test AI bid recommendations against forty completed supplier orders
Complete the supplier-audit course only if the director pays the hours
Apply for posted goods-checking work only if wages cover the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for dates and written terms for every buyer whose work ends. I’d tell suppliers they still need a named person to call about a missing shipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my job is comparing and deciding, so I expect the desk to go when AGI arrives in 2028. Physical loading work may last until robots come around 2031, but Mei’s preschool wage alone cannot cover our mortgage and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This weekend Mei and I would cancel the planned garden shed and keep the deposit in cash. Before 2028 I’d ask the warehouse manager about paid goods-inspection vacancies and enroll in a forklift safety course only if the company pays for both fee and time; after AGI arrives, I’d take a posted inspection job only if the written wage meets our mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed because two years leaves very little room for a new skill. Three months saved is not enough to carry us through a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family to help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would help if they could, but I would first ask what they can actually spare. I would not turn our mortgage into their monthly bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the warehouse wage is lower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the current job while it exists and search other nearby firms. I will not trade a working wage for a title painted on a loading-bay door.

say: I’d seek **written job dates** for the buying team.
Suppliers need a **named shipment contact** after desk changes.
think: Warehouse work faces **2031 robots**, while Mei’s wage cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: Cancel the **garden shed** and hold its deposit in cash.
Seek **paid inspection vacancies** and enroll in funded forklift training before 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the short training window.
S2.quote: I will not trade a working wage for a title painted on a loading-bay door.
fieldNote: His desk work faces the **2028 thinking deadline** directly.
He sees warehouse work as a **short bridge** before 2031 robots.
The move requires a **posted written wage** and funded training time.

steps.text: Cancel the planned garden shed and retain the deposit for household bills
Enroll in forklift safety training only if the company pays fee and time
Ask the warehouse manager about paid goods-inspection vacancies before 2028
Take a posted inspection role after 2028 only if written pay covers the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives a firm time to show which warehouse places are real and pay people to learn safely. I’d want the numbers posted, not whispered around the loading bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep my pay while I qualify for goods inspection before 2031. Robots for physical work follow around 2034, so I would need to keep looking beyond that first warehouse job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d enroll in a paid warehouse inspection certificate only if Mei can handle school pickup on the two late days. I’d shadow the receiving team on paid time, then apply for a posted inspector vacancy before 2031 if its wage meets our mortgage; after AGI arrives, I’d stay only while paid human checks still happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but less pressed than in 2028. I can see whether the work suits me before giving up a manager’s paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mei cannot do both pickups?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my brother whether he can cover one, but I would check with Mei before making the plan. I would postpone the course rather than leave our youngest waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expect robots to leave inspection alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Around 2034 they could check boxes too, so I would use the extra time to keep our savings intact.

say: I’d demand **posted warehouse openings** and paid learning.
The company has time to show **real numbers** before cuts.
think: I can qualify before **2031 AGI** while drawing pay.
The **2034 robots** could also take physical inspection tasks.
do: Enroll in a **paid certificate** only with covered school pickups.
Shadow **receiving work** on paid time and seek a mortgage-covering opening.
Stay in **inspection work** after 2031 only while paid human checks remain.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can test the site work.
S3.quote: I would postpone the course rather than leave our youngest waiting.
fieldNote: He treats **childcare** as a gate to evening training.
His shadowing needs **paid time** before any move.
He knows **2034 robots** may take physical inspection too.

steps.text: Enroll in paid warehouse training only after arranging two late pickups with Mei
Shadow the receiving team during paid working hours
Apply for a posted inspector role before 2031 only if wages cover the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years lets employers offer real apprenticeships instead of short courses that lead nowhere. I’d ask for written dates and wages before people leave buying jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could pay down part of the mortgage and build a larger reserve by 2036 if Mei and I keep our hours. I would be 53 then, so starting over without a plan would be harder. A receiving lead still plans and checks orders, and those thinking tasks face AGI in 2036; physical checks face robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 Mei and I would raise our savings transfer to 170 monthly only while both paychecks are steady. I’d take a paid warehouse course once the site offers an actual training place, and apply for a posted receiving lead job before 2036 only if the wage covers the mortgage; in the first year after AGI, I’d stay only while it remains paid human work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the date, but the long run gives us room to make one careful move. I would rather earn a place on the floor than chase a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course with no vacancy attached?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would ask the site manager what openings it has actually filled before spending time away from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Dad is learning work that may change his shifts, but their school day still comes first. I would ask Mei before promising any late evenings.

say: Employers should offer **real apprenticeships** with actual openings.
Workers deserve **written dates and wages** before leaving buying work.
think: A decade could build **savings** and reduce debt.
At **53**, I would want a tested role before leaving management.
A receiving lead’s **planning tasks** face 2036 AI before physical checks face 2039 robots.
do: Save **170 monthly** only while both paychecks are steady.
Take **paid warehouse training** and apply for receiving work only at mortgage-covering pay.
Keep the **receiving role** after 2036 only while it remains paid human work.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but can make a careful move.
S4.quote: I would rather earn a place on the floor than chase a title.
fieldNote: He requires **real site openings** before using family time for a course.
The higher savings transfer depends on **two steady paychecks**.
His receiving move still needs **paid work** after 2036.
A receiving lead’s **desk tasks** remain exposed at 2036 AGI despite hands-on work continuing longer.

steps.text: Transfer 170 monthly into savings only while both household paychecks remain steady
Complete paid warehouse training only after the site offers an actual place
Apply for a posted receiving lead role before 2036 only if wages cover the mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My job is mostly contracts and judgment, and a warehouse wage might not cover the mortgage. A funded course with paid time, a posted opening and written pay would help me choose honestly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who tells a supplier a truck is late when the bid office closes. A signed promise still needs somebody to stand beside the empty loading bay.

headlineQuote: A signed promise still needs somebody to stand beside the empty loading bay.
portrait: **Colin**, 43, is a new supplier-bids manager with a bachelor’s degree.
Typical pay and **three months saved** support a mortgage and two children.
He uses AI **occasionally** after a colleague proves it against real bids.
He seeks **paid warehouse training** only with childcare, a vacancy and mortgage-covering wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close his thinking-heavy bid desk before a viable warehouse route opens.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded course**, paid training time, posted opening and written wage would help him choose.
